processing_steps.processing_steps_notes: 50 kg ingots of the steel were prepared by induction melting under an argon atmosphere.
Homogenization at the same (forging) temperature for 3 h prior to hot rolling.
Hot rolled after homogenization at 1200 °C for 3 h to a thickness of 3.5 mm with a reduction of 90%.
The hot-rolled strips were annealed at 1000 °C for 1 h.
Cold rolled to a thickness of 1 mm.
The cold rolled strips were annealed at 1000 °C, followed by water quenching to room temperature, producing the as-quenched terminal state studied in this work.

Tensile tests were carried out at room temperature using a universal testing machine (SANSCMT5000) at a constant crosshead displacement velocity equivalent to an initial strain rate of 1.33 × 10^-3 s^-1.

structures.overall_structure: As-quenched 0.5C steel has a duplex ferritic–austenitic microstructure. Optical microscopy shows a strongly banded duplex structure in which dark-grey, elongated and discontinuous second-phase bands lie roughly horizontally inside a lighter grey matrix, with grain boundaries visible in the light regions (Fig. 1(a)). The austenite volume fraction is 59.2%. Detailed TEM analysis reveals that no precipitates exist in either the austenite or the ferrite phase of the 0.5C steel.

defects.type: dislocation tangles around subgrain/cell boundaries (true strain ε = 0.02)

structures.overall_structure: Microstructural evolution of the 0.5C steel during tensile deformation (interrupted tests + TEM): planar slip traces and dislocation tangles at low strain (ε = 0.02), then intensive dislocation slip, Taylor lattice and microbands in austenite together with dense dislocation tangles in ferrite at ε = 0.18, corresponding to the two-stage strain hardening behaviour.

defects.type: planar slip traces at ε = 0.02; intensive dislocation slip, Taylor lattice and microbands at ε = 0.18
dislocation tangles at ε = 0.02; dense dislocation tangles at ε = 0.18

defect_interactions.interaction_type: dislocation substructure development (planar slip → Taylor lattice/microbands)
defect_interactions.qualitative_or_quantitative_description: In the second deformation stage a low energy Taylor lattice structure, equivalent to dislocation tangles in wavy-slip materials, and microbands develop in austenite, resulting in a relatively high strain hardening.
Dislocation tangles form in ferrite in the first stage and increase to dense dislocation tangles in the second stage of deformation.

interfaces.slip_behavior: Planar slip starts in austenite at low strain (ε = 0.02) while dislocation tangles form in ferrite; at ε = 0.18 intensive dislocation slip, a Taylor lattice and microbands develop in austenite and dense dislocation tangles form in ferrite.
interfaces.interface_notes: The C–J analysis can describe the strain hardening behaviour of the duplex Fe–18Mn–10Al–0.5C steel because the difference in hardness between ferrite and austenite is not quite obvious, so the increase in strain can reflect the strain hardening behaviour of the 0.5C steel.

measurement_conditions.other_conditions: Uniaxial tensile tests on a universal testing machine (SANSCMT5000) at a constant crosshead displacement velocity equivalent to an initial strain rate of 1.33 × 10^-3 s^-1.

tensile_properties.stress_strain_curves: Engineering stress–strain curve of the 0.5C steel (Fig. 3): peak just above the 800 MPa gridline, fracture at an engineering strain a little past 0.3; no visible yield-point drop.

strain_hardening_rate.value: Two-stage strain hardening (Crussard–Jaoul analysis); breakpoint at true strain ε = 0.025; strain hardening rate decays fastest of the three steels and reaches zero closest to a strain of 0.3

characterization_methods.instrument_or_setup: Standard mechanical polishing followed by etching with a solution of 1 ml hydrochloric acid, 100 ml methanol and 4 g picric acid
characterization_methods.measurement_conditions: As-quenched specimens; 40 µm scale bar used for imaging
characterization_methods.purpose: To observe the as-quenched optical microstructures of the Fe–18Mn–10Al–xC steels
characterization_methods.key_findings: 0.5C steel shows a banded duplex ferritic–austenitic structure with dark-grey elongated discontinuous bands inside a lighter grey matrix (Fig. 1(a)).

characterization_methods.purpose: To measure the volume fractions of different phases
characterization_methods.key_findings: Austenite volume fraction of the 0.5C steel is 59.2%.

characterization_methods.technique: transmission electron microscopy (TEM), including selected-area diffraction (SADP)
characterization_methods.instrument_or_setup: Tecnai G2 20 TEM at an acceleration voltage of 200 kV; thin foils prepared by twinjet electropolishing in 9% perchloric acid in methanol at −30 °C
characterization_methods.measurement_conditions: As-quenched thin foils; bright- and dark-field imaging with SADP
characterization_methods.purpose: To identify phases and precipitates and to characterize the deformation substructure
characterization_methods.key_findings: No precipitates exist in either austenite (Fig. 2(a)) or ferrite (Fig. 2(b)) of the 0.5C steel; the austenite SADP (020, 111, 1̄11) shows no extra reflections.

characterization_methods.measurement_conditions: Room temperature; constant crosshead displacement velocity equivalent to an initial strain rate of 1.33 × 10^-3 s^-1
characterization_methods.purpose: To measure the tensile properties (YS, UTS, TE) and the engineering stress–strain curves

characterization_methods.measurement_conditions: Applied to the tensile flow data of the as-quenched 0.5C steel
characterization_methods.purpose: To analyze the strain hardening behaviour and identify its stages
characterization_methods.key_findings: The 0.5C steel exhibits a two-stage strain hardening behaviour with a breakpoint at true strain ε = 0.025 (Fig. 5(a)).

computational_details.simulation_method: Empirical/analytical calculation of steel density from chemical composition

analytical_models.equation_role: Calculation of the density of the Fe–18Mn–10Al–xC steels from composition
analytical_models.model_note: Densities of the three steels were calculated as 6.92, 6.88 and 6.78 g/cm3; the 0.5C steel value is 6.92 g/cm3.

computational_details.simulation_method: Thermodynamic/analytical calculation of austenite stacking fault energy (SFE)
computational_details.potential_model_or_database: SFE model used previously by the authors, Ref. [13]

analytical_models.equation_role: Calculation of the stacking fault energy of austenite from alloy composition
analytical_models.model_note: The SFE of austenite in the 0.5C steel is 73.4 mJ/m2 (1.2C steel: 84.5 mJ/m2).

unmapped_findings: The 0.5C steel has a duplex ferritic–austenitic structure with an austenite volume fraction of 59.2%; no precipitates exist in either the austenite or the ferrite phase of the 0.5C steel.
The calculated density of the 0.5C steel is 6.92 g/cm3 and the calculated austenite stacking fault energy (SFE) is 73.4 mJ/m2 (0.8C: 6.88 g/cm3 / 77.9 mJ/m2; 1.2C: 6.78 g/cm3 / 84.5 mJ/m2).
The product of ultimate tensile strength and total elongation (UTS × TE) for the 0.5C steel is 28100 MPa·%, the lowest of the three steels (0.8C: 37597; 1.2C: 53205).

The C–J analysis can describe the strain hardening behaviour of the duplex Fe–18Mn–10Al–0.5C steel because the features of ferrite and martensite are quite different (and the increase in stress in martensite dominates strain hardening), whereas the difference in hardness between ferrite and austenite is not quite obvious.
Measured chemical composition of the 0.5C steel (mass %): Al 9.90, Mn 17.71, C 0.48, Fe balance (Table 1).
